page: Amazon Web Services r6id.metal is a bare-metal, memory-optimized server instance built on the x86_64 architecture. The platform features dual-socket Intel Xeon Platinum 8375C processors running at a 3.5 GHz clock speed, delivering 64 physical cores and 128 dedicated execution threads with Hyper-Threading. The processor incorporates 54 MB of shared L3 cache, alongside specialized instruction sets including AVX-512, VAES, and Intel Total Memory Encryption. The hardware configuration supplies 1024 GB of DDR4 system memory clocked at 3 GHz, providing an 8:1 memory-to-core allocation ratio. Peripheral hardware includes 7600 GB of attached local NVMe SSD storage and 50 Gbps baseline networking throughput.

Benchmark measurements reflect high resource density and robust parallelism. In compute-intensive tests, the server achieves top-tier results in PassMark CPU tests (88,191.68) and PassMark extended instructions (109,743.58), alongside strong multi-core outcomes across stress-ng (124,966.04) and Geekbench multi-core (17,782.0). Single-core metrics in stress-ng and Geekbench place in the middle 50% tier, highlighting a configuration designed for aggregate throughput rather than isolated single-thread frequency. Memory subsystems demonstrate high uncached throughput, yielding 338.87 GB/sec in 256MB read tests and 132.33 GB/sec in large-block writes.

In operational and memory-bound tests, r6id.metal sustained 110.69 million Redis SET operations per second and strong PassMark database scores. While small and medium LLM prompt processing shows strong throughput via AVX-512 execution, token generation rates remain modest due to the absence of dedicated GPU acceleration. The combination of direct hardware access, high memory density, NVMe instance store volumes, and 50 Gbps networking positions this server for in-memory databases, large-scale caching tiers, transactional workloads, and big data analytics pipelines requiring high local IOPS without hypervisor overhead.

The combination of bare-metal control, extensive volatile memory, and large NVMe instance storage makes this configuration well suited for large in-memory key-value databases, real-time analytics, and transactional data architectures requiring sustained I/O performance.
